qs.q: A 35-year-old man presents with acute hepatitis symptoms. Laboratory workup confirms Hepatitis A virus infection. Through which primary mechanism is Hepatitis A typically transmitted?
o: Feco-oral transmission via contaminated water or food
Parenteral exposure to infected blood products
Vertical transmission from mother to newborn child
qs.e: Hepatitis A is transmitted via the feco-oral route through contaminated water, food, or close personal contact. Parenteral and sexual routes are the primary modes for Hepatitis B and C.

qs.q: NOT a symptom of acute hepatitis A?
qs.e: Anorexia (loss of appetite), not an increase, is typical.
qs.s: Medical Virology CAT 2024/2025 — MKU MBMM 3333 MCQs with Answers

qs.e: HAV is transmitted exclusively by the fecal-oral route — contaminated water, raw shellfish, unwashed produce, and poor hand hygiene. It is a non-enveloped virus, making it resistant to environmental conditions. Unlike HBV/HCV, it is NOT sexually transmitted or bloodborne as a primary route.

qs.q: A 20-year-old male presents with anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and RUQ pain. He has a history of intravenous drug use and multiple sexual partners. Serological tests are negative for Hepatitis A, B, and C. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
qs.e: Given the history of intravenous drug use and multiple sexual partners, drug-induced liver injury (DILI) is a strong possibility. While Hepatitis E can cause acute hepatitis, it's typically acquired through contaminated water or food and less common in this demographic. Autoimmune hepatitis is a possibility but less likely without specific autoantibodies. Budd-Chiari syndrome involves hepatic vein obstruction.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Hepatitis A is an acute, self‑limiting viral infection transmitted fecal‑oral, presenting with jaundice and malaise. Diagnosis hinges on anti‑HAV IgM; management is supportive, with vaccination for prevention.

sections.p: Hepatitis A is caused by a non‑enveloped, single‑stranded RNA virus of the Picornaviridae family. It is acute, never becomes chronic, and is diagnosed by detecting anti‑HAV IgM antibodies in serum.

t.b: Positive indicates acute infection; negative suggests past exposure or vaccination.
Elevated in jaundice; mixed pattern with >70% unconjugated.
Markedly raised, peak 10–20× ULN in acute phase.
Usually normal; low levels may hint at severe hepatic dysfunction.

sections.p: Acute hepatitis A is classified by clinical severity: mild (no symptoms), moderate (jaundice, fatigue), severe (fulminant hepatic failure). Fulminant cases are rare but life‑threatening.
Primary route is fecal‑oral transmission via contaminated food or water. Other risk factors include poor sanitation, travel to endemic areas, and close contact with infected individuals.
Patients develop a prodrome of fatigue, nausea, and abdominal discomfort, followed by jaundice. Hepatomegaly and mild right upper quadrant tenderness may be present.
Baseline labs include liver function tests, coagulation profile, and serology for hepatitis A, B, and C. Imaging is reserved for atypical presentations.

t.b: Elevated INR indicates impaired synthetic function; monitor for bleeding risk.
Low levels may predict severe disease.

sections.p: Complications are uncommon but include fulminant hepatic failure, hepatic encephalopathy, and rarely, extra‑hepatic manifestations such as hemolytic anemia.
Supportive care is the mainstay: adequate hydration, nutrition, and monitoring of liver function. Antiviral therapy is not indicated. Avoid hepatotoxic drugs and alcohol.
b: Hydration with oral or IV fluids

sections.p: Patients recover fully; most develop lifelong immunity. Vaccination is recommended for travelers, MSM, and people with chronic liver disease.
b: Post‑infection serology: anti‑HAV IgG indicates immunity

t.b: Positive confirms immunity; no further risk.

sections.p: Acute viral hepatitis B or C, alcoholic hepatitis, and drug‑induced liver injury can mimic HAV but differ in serology and chronicity.
Early in infection, anti‑HAV IgM may be negative; ALT can be normal in mild cases. A normal bilirubin does not exclude HAV if the patient is early.

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of fulminant hepatic failure: altered mental status, severe coagulopathy, persistent vomiting, or abdominal pain with hypotension.

faq.a: No, HAV infection is always acute and self‑limited.

faq.q: Is vaccination safe for pregnant women?
faq.a: Yes, the inactivated HAV vaccine is safe and recommended for pregnant travelers.
